_comment: Targets your LUMINA deployment must meet, declared BEFORE the first run, plus the cost model bench.mjs uses. Two gears, two envelopes: quick is the default and must stay cheap and fast; deep may cost and take several times more, and has to earn it. Tune the workload to your corpus; do not loosen the gates to pass. PRICES ARE PLACEHOLDERS: set them to your providers' published rates before trusting the dollar figures.

_sla_notes.ttft_p95_ms: quick search: the 'it's thinking' window a user tolerates
_sla_notes.answer_p95_ms: quick search, end to end: plan + 2 searches + 4 fetches + synthesis
_sla_notes.deep_plan_p95_ms: deep search streams its plan before it retrieves anything, so this is deep's real first-paint. A deep search that shows nothing for 30s reads as broken however good the answer is.
_sla_notes.deep_answer_p95_s: deep search, end to end. Perplexity-class deep research takes a minute; the cap keeps it from taking five.
_sla_notes.min_deep_sub_questions: a plan with two sub-questions is a quick search with extra steps
_sla_notes.min_deep_source_ratio: distinct sources in a deep answer over the same query answered quick. Deep that reads no more than quick is only slower, and this is the number that catches it.
_sla_notes.max_cost_per_deep_answer_usd: deep is allowed to cost ~7x quick. It is not allowed to be unbounded, which is why it also sits behind a per-user daily cap.
